title: The Devil's Handwriting: Ludovico Spoletano's conjuration, Teseo Ambrogio, Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam (Pavia 1539), f. 212v

steps.what: Searched the repository, catalogue.json and the web (Schmeh's Encrypted Book List, Cipher Mysteries) for the image or a description of it.

Compared the signs with rendered charts of Samaritan, Phoenician, Ethiopic, Glagolitic, Tibetan, Old Italic, Old Hungarian, Georgian and Armenian; Ethiopic fits best (arch letters, ተ, ገ, ለ, አ, ። and numeral bars), Samaritan second; the commonest sign has no clear counterpart.
Tested the image rotated 180 degrees as upside-down Latin script.
Segmented the glyphs automatically and transcribed 174 signs into provisional classes from contact sheets.
Simple substitution into Latin (CLTK Caesar/Cicero/Sallust quadgrams), 12 annealing restarts, one-to-one key on the commonest classes.
Same solver on three shuffles of the transcription: shuffled -12.46 to -12.62 per quadgram against real -12.86, so the Latin fit is no better than chance.
Scheers PDF identified the target as Ambrogio 1539 f. 212v (Devil's Handwriting); searches confirm no published decipherment.
Compared further scripts (Hangul, kana with 90-degree rotation, Brahmi, Batak, Rejang, Hanunoo, Canadian syllabics, Tifinagh, Armenian, mirror and 180-degree readings).
Simple substitution of own transcription into Hebrew, Croatian, Russian, Amharic consonant rows, Latin and Italian, both directions.
Ethiopic visual consonant values with free vowels, scored against Italian and Latin; z = 0.27 / 0.33 against permuted values.
Scheers transcription, simple substitution into Latin and Italian: beats 15 shuffles (z about 4.5 and 2.8).
Bigram (Markov-1) surrogates of the Scheers transcription score as well or better, so the excess over shuffles comes from sign-pair habits, not language.
Calibration on 153 letters of Caesar: plain substitution solved (LM -9.0 to -9.7); with 6 homophones (25 signs) not solved by the same or a frequency-penalised homophonic solver.
Calibrated homophonic solver (C, 5-gram, 24 restarts x 3M): solves 6/6 held-out Latin and 6/6 held-out Italian 153-letter 31-sign controls (88-100%), scores -1.62 to -2.12.

Same solver on the Devil's text (Scheers and own transcription, both directions): Latin -2.37/-2.50, Italian -2.44/-2.45, inside the shuffle range -2.42 to -2.52; Hebrew, Spanish, French, German, Greek, Arabic, Amharic rows, vowel-dropped and vowel-merged Italian/Latin also at shuffle level.
17 Italian/Latin cribs from the question at every offset (15,970 placements, 2,449 consistent) with the calibrated solver; best -2.50, nowhere near solved-control scores (-1.6 to -2.1).

Machine segmentation (183 glyphs) and HOG clustering, then glyph-by-glyph labels: transcription_v3.txt, 161 signs, 38 classes; agrees with the first transcription. Calibrated solver on it: Italian -2.31, Latin -2.38, shuffles -2.34 to -2.37.

Abugida model (one consonant per sign family, one vowel per mark class) calibrated on Italian syllabary controls (3/4 solved); on the Devil's text Italian and Latin, both directions, -2.51 to -2.55 against shuffles -2.49 to -2.54.

Amadi's Letere diaboliche (c. 1588, redrawn by Scheers): 31 demon-named signs matching the woodcut's sign set; first letters of the names as values give no words, z = 1.35 (Italian) / 0.63 (Latin) against 2,000 random reassignments.

Read Ambrogio's own account (ff. 212r-213r, archive.org scan): the conjurer was later killed by peasants 'with as many iron tridents as the invoked Amon had drawn in his characters' (tot ferris tridentibus, quot invocatus Amon in suis characteribus effinxerat); the commonest sign (sideways E with long bar) is a trident, so the source's only meaning for the characters is a pictorial omen, consistent with the absence of any linguistic plaintext.

Houston and Rojas (2024) checked: they transcribe and translate the f. 212v-213r passage including the trident sentence and call the signs a 'pitchfork script', but treat them as a possible alphabet; the omen reading and the null tests are new here.

validation.notes: no reading: not a cipher; the tests are calibrated null results recorded in NOTES (matched controls and shuffles), not a key to validate

outcome.method_basis: Ambrogio's own account (f. 213r) gives the characters one meaning, a pictorial omen: the conjurer was later killed by peasants 'with as many iron tridents as the invoked Amon had drawn in his characters'; the commonest sign is a trident, and no letter-substitution plaintext exists in eleven languages under three transcriptions, with solvers that solve matched controls.
outcome.notes: Not a cipher on the evidence of the source and the tests: the characters depict tridents (an omen of the conjurer's death), not a text. A code of whole words or a meaningless pseudo-script cannot be excluded in principle; no linguistic content was found.
